title: Infinite UI Agents
lesson_url_note: Public YouTube upload of the lesson; the codebase (agentic-horizon-extras/ui-agents) is an exclusive Agentic Horizon member asset — the third in the trilogy ceo-agents → lead-agents → ui-agents. There is no standalone public course page for this asset.

video.youtube_title: My Pi Agent Teams. Claude Code Leak SIGNAL. Harness Engineering
official_chapters: 14:37 Control the Harness - Control your Results

tactic.name: Own the Harness (Harness Engineering)
tactic.one_liner: Stop solving one-off tasks with a single agent. Own the agent harness and engineer specialized teams of agents inside it, so you solve entire problem classes on your behalf — because the harness, not the model, is where the durable leverage lives.
tactic.why_uncomfortable: The whole industry just finished adopting Claude Code — a single, powerful agent — and this tactic tells you that isn't the edge anymore. It asks you to accept that models are being commoditized and that the durable value (a $2.5B ARR signal from the Claude Code source-code leak) sits in the layer beneath the model: the harness (deterministic code, token caching, agent orchestration, prompts, skills, model control). It then asks you to leave the mainstream tool for a more granular one (the Pi coding agent) to build and specialize your own harness — more moving parts, more to maintain, a bet on tooling outside the herd. And it demands trust: handing an entire product domain to a team of agents you did not hand-hold, betting they will observe, act, learn, and iterate like you would. That is a bigger leap than prompting one agent to build one thing.

mission: Scale your compute to scale your impact. Become the engineer who builds specialized systems of agents that operate whole product domains — better than your coworkers, better than you can — capturing fractions of the value the Claude Code leak revealed lives in the agent harness. The North Star is agents that operate your product end to end while you sleep: not cron jobs, but teams of agents that run the product. You get there by owning the core four (context, model, prompt, tools) at the harness level and increasing, over time, the trust you place in your agents to do larger and larger scales of work.

levels_model.vibe_coding: Prompt a model to generate code. The lowest-hanging fruit; produces outdated, inefficient codebases at scale. Dan: 'you are the bottleneck.'
levels_model.agentic_coding_single_agent: One agent (Claude Code) running long tool chains to do engineering work. Powerful, now mainstream — 'Claude Code is everywhere. It is now the mainstream.' Still one instance, one problem at a time.
levels_model.harness_engineering_teams: You own the agent harness and engineer teams of specialized, learning agents that a single orchestrator commands. You stop solving one-off tasks and start operating entire problem classes. This is the phase-two move of this lesson: single agent → owned multi-team harness.

harness_definition.what_it_is: The agent harness is everything around the model that makes agents possible. Dan enumerates six components the Claude Code leak put a spotlight on.
harness_definition.load_bearing_claim: Without the agent harness there are no agents, no agentic coding, and therefore no agentic engineering. Anthropic created the category and got first-mover advantage — but the model on top is being commoditized, so the harness is the product and harness engineering is the skill.
harness_definition.in_this_repo: The Pi harness config is tiny and legible: .pi/settings.json exposes thinking: 'high', autoCompact: true, compactThreshold: 0.8, and prompts: ['./prompts/multi-team']. Per-agent model/tools/domain/skills live in each agent's front matter. That surface — thinking budget, context compaction, prompt registration, per-agent core-four control — is what 'owning the harness' concretely buys you here.

core_concepts.name: The agent harness is the product (the Claude Code leak signal)
core_concepts.plain_english: When Claude Code's source leaked, most engineers chased the features and the new model. The real signal is that a $2.5B ARR business is built on the harness — the deterministic code, token caching, orchestration, prompts, skills, and model control around the model. The model is being commoditized; the harness is the durable asset.
core_concepts.dan_words: "The Claude code leak tells us that the agent harness is the product. Of course, they pioneered a great model that runs on top of it, but as you know, the models are being quickly commoditized."
core_concepts.misconception: That the lesson is a hot-take on the leak. It is the opposite of a hot-take: the point is not the leaked features or the 'Mythos model,' it is a structural signal you can act on — go learn to build harnesses.

core_concepts.name: Harness engineering — the highest-leverage skill
core_concepts.plain_english: Take a tool that gives you granular control (Dan uses the Pi coding agent) and build an agent harness specialized for your domain. Owning the harness gives you an edge over everyone still using the stock mainstream tool, and lets you capture fractions of the value the leak exposed.
core_concepts.dan_words: "One of the most viable skills an agentic engineer can learn is harness engineering. When you stop vibe coding and you start agentic engineering teams of agents in your agent harness, you can solve problem classes, not just one-off tasks."
core_concepts.misconception: That harness engineering means abandoning Claude Code. Dan is explicit: 'in ands not ors.' He spends ~80% of his time in Claude Code as a meta-builder and runs the specialized Pi harness to operate the product.

core_concepts.name: Solve problem classes, not one-off tasks
core_concepts.plain_english: There is little value in prompting an agent to build the thing. The move is to build a team of agents that knows how to build (and operate) that whole class of things on your behalf. Because 80–90% of engineering and knowledge work is a workflow — a series of tasks — you systematize the workflow once and run it forever.
core_concepts.dan_words: "There is very little value in prompting your agent to build the thing. What you want to be doing instead is thinking about how you can build a system of agents, specifically a team of agents, that knows how to build the application on your behalf, that knows how to operate that domain on your behalf."
core_concepts.misconception: That this is just 'reusable prompts.' It is a level up: the prompt targets a whole team that already understands the domain, so one command (e.g. /generate) drives an end-to-end workflow, not a single generation.

core_concepts.name: Three-tier orchestration: orchestrator → leads → workers
core_concepts.plain_english: The system has one orchestrator, several team leads, and many hyper-specialized workers. Orchestrator and leads are thinkers, planners, managers, delegators — they do not write files. Workers are the doers; they write the files. Maximum value comes from this separation.
core_concepts.dan_words: "Our orchestrator and our leads don't do any work. They're thinkers, they're managers, they're leaders, most importantly, they're delegators... they delegate the building to the actual worker levels."
core_concepts.misconception: That leads/orchestrator are a bottleneck doing nothing. Their job is classification, routing, and synthesis — and in this repo the rule is enforced structurally: leads/orchestrator have a `delegate` tool but their `domain` permissions block writing product files (they may only upsert their own mental model).

core_concepts.name: One orchestrator interface — input must not scale with agent count
core_concepts.plain_english: You talk to a single orchestrator, no matter how many agents are behind it. If your effort to drive the system grew with every agent you added, the human would become the bottleneck. So teams scale horizontally, but your interface stays one chat with one orchestrator.
core_concepts.dan_words: "With our teams of agents, we need to make sure that our input to the system doesn't scale with the number of agents that we have. This directly limits what you can do. So, we have horizontal scaling of all of our agent teams, but we are always just going through a single orchestrator agent."
core_concepts.misconception: That more agents means more prompting for you. The whole design goal is the reverse: add compute (agents/teams) without adding human input.

core_concepts.name: Own the core four (context, model, prompt, tools) in the harness
core_concepts.plain_english: Agentic control is still the core four — context, model, prompt, tools. Owning the harness is what lets you push and specialize each of them per agent, instead of accepting a stock tool's defaults. In this repo that control lives in each agent's front matter.
core_concepts.dan_words: "What I'm doing here is gaining full control over the core four context model prompt and tools. And to gain maximum control, you really need control of the agent harness."
core_concepts.misconception: That the core four became obsolete. They are still the whole game — the harness just moves the controls into your hands, per agent, at scale.

core_concepts.name: Specialization via front matter — one agent, one prompt, one purpose
core_concepts.plain_english: Each agent's YAML front matter is where the magic happens: an expertise file (its persistent mental model), hot-loaded skills (injected behavior), a tools list (its capabilities), and a domain (the exact paths it may operate on). Narrow, focused context — one agent, one prompt, one purpose — is a massive advantage in multi-agent systems.
core_concepts.dan_words: "The front matter is where a lot of the magic happens... Specialization and that focused context window, one agent, one prompt, one purpose, is a massive advantage in these multi-agent team systems."
core_concepts.misconception: That specialization is just a system prompt. It is four coordinated controls (expertise + skills + tools + domain). The `domain` field is the sleeper: it path-scopes where an agent can read/upsert/delete, which is what actually makes 'front-end-only' or 'billing-only' agents real.

core_concepts.name: Agents that learn — persistent mental models
core_concepts.plain_english: Each agent maintains its own YAML expertise file — its mental model of the system — that compounds across sessions. A tiny skill teaches it how to read the file at task start and update it after work. The human never touches the file; the agent decides what to track. Teams of agents that remember.
core_concepts.dan_words: "The agent operates, controls, and tracks whatever it thinks it needs to. I don't touch this file ever. All I've done here is give this agent a skill, which very, very simply tells it how to manage its mental model."
core_concepts.misconception: That the mental models ship pre-filled. In the committed repo all 12 expertise files are one-line stubs (`# Mental model — auto-maintained by agent`); the ~7K-token, dated mental model Dan shows on screen is runtime-accumulated state, not committed. The front matter caps growth at max-lines: 10000.

core_concepts.name: Model control and reliability — heterogeneous models, graceful failure
core_concepts.plain_english: Owning the harness lets you assign a different model to each agent or team and swap them at will. Dan runs open-source models (Minimax M2.7, Step 3.5 Flash) on teams A and B next to Claude Sonnet 4.6 on team C. The open-source teams fail silently mid-demo — so the leads (Claude) break the 'don't write files' rule and finish the work themselves. Redundancy across models and teams is what keeps the pipeline delivering.
core_concepts.dan_words: "Just another reason to have multiple teams and different models running... I could easily add a model rotation system into this if needed. So, if this model is not working, swap it out. So, there's all types of things you can do when you own the agent harness."
core_concepts.misconception: That the demo failing is a flaw in the idea. The failure is the argument: because Dan owns the harness, a broken model is survivable — another model/team picks up the work, and the harness could rotate models automatically. The README's 'Recommended: use Claude series models... proven reliable' is exactly why the open-source teams struggled.

core_concepts.name: The till-done list
core_concepts.plain_english: Not a to-do list, not a to-done list — a till-done list. The orchestrator opens a titled task list, adds discrete verifiable items each owned by a team, and the system works until every task is complete.
core_concepts.dan_words: "We now have a not a to-do list, not a to-done list, we have a till-done list. So, our agents are going to work until all these tasks are complete."
core_concepts.misconception: That till-done is baked into the /generate prompt. It is an orchestrator capability: `tilldone` is one of the orchestrator's tools (see orchestrator.md), used autonomously for substantial work. The committed generate.md deliberately omits a task list (per specs/parallel-team-duplication.md) to stress-test coordination; on screen the orchestrator still spins one up ([1/8] → [11/11]).

core_concepts.name: Reusable prompts composed against your teams
core_concepts.plain_english: Because you own the team, you can write reusable prompts (commands) that drive the whole team through a workflow top to bottom. /generate takes brand, product, tree, count, and a brief; the orchestrator runs the 8-step pipeline. Prompts use information-dense keywords — 'delegate' is literally a tool — and a consistent Variables / Instructions / Workflow / Report shape.
core_concepts.dan_words: "Delegate is literally a tool. We're using information-dense keywords inside of our workflows to communicate maximum information... 80% of engineering work and of knowledge work, frankly, probably 90% is a workflow. It's a series of tasks."
core_concepts.misconception: That composing prompts against agents is exotic. Dan notes you can do it in Claude Code too, the moment you build your own agents — it just becomes far more powerful once you own a whole team and harness.

core_concepts.name: Claude Code as the meta agent
core_concepts.plain_english: Dan spends ~80% of his time in Claude Code, but mostly not on the product itself — he uses it as a meta-builder to build the systems (teams of agents, AI developer workflows) that then operate the product. Claude Code builds the system that builds the system; the specialized Pi harness runs the product.
core_concepts.dan_words: "I'm using Cloud Code as a meta builder, a meta agent. When I'm in Cloud Code usually I'm building the system that builds the system."
core_concepts.misconception: That owning a harness means dropping Claude Code. 'In ands not ors' — Claude Code is the meta-agent that constructs and improves the specialized system you then run.

core_concepts.name: Trust and scale — the theme of 2026
core_concepts.plain_english: Harness engineering and multi-agent orchestration are the two big skills; trust and scale underline both. The point of the harness is to increase, over time, the trust you place in your agents to do ever-larger scales of work — until they operate your product end to end.
core_concepts.dan_words: "The theme of 2026 is increasing the trust you have in your agents to do larger scales of work over time."
core_concepts.misconception: That scale alone is the goal. Scale without trust is noise; the pairing is the point — you build closed, specialized systems specifically so you can trust them at larger scale.

core_concepts.name: Agentic security — the demo domain and a business opening
core_concepts.plain_english: The demo brand, Aegis, is an 'agent security command center.' Dan flags agents + security as one of the biggest engineering business opportunities of the next few years: anyone can now prompt an exploit, so defensive agents that watch logs and detect anomalies in real time will be essential.
core_concepts.dan_words: "The agentic security space is going to be one of the most important business opportunities for engineers... because anyone can sit down right now and just write a prompt to exploit an application."
core_concepts.misconception: That Aegis is the lesson. Aegis is the demo domain that proves the system generalizes; the lesson is the harness and multi-team orchestration that produced it. Any brand/domain would do.

core_four_in_the_harness.context: Per-agent, controlled two ways: shared_context in multi-team-config.yaml (README, CLAUDE.md, the _template brand.yaml/trees.yaml, and the two Zod schemas — the files every agent sees) plus each agent's own expertise file (its accumulating mental model) and its runtime session log/conversation log. Narrow, purpose-built context per agent is the whole design.
core_four_in_the_harness.model: Per-agent in front matter (`model:` key). The committed agents are uniformly `anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6`; CLAUDE.md recommends Claude series (claude-sonnet-4-6, claude-opus-4-6). On screen Dan swaps open-source models into specific agents (Vue Generator → stepfun/step-3.5-flash; Vue Generator (B) → openrouter/minimax/minimax-m2.7) to A/B them against Sonnet — the harness makes per-agent model choice trivial and rotatable.
core_four_in_the_harness.prompt: Two layers: the agent system prompts (Purpose / Variables / Instructions, with injected {{...}} blocks) and the reusable team prompts in .pi/prompts/multi-team/ (Variables / Instructions / Workflow / Report). The prompt graduates from 'build this' to a workflow specification that delegates across teams.
core_four_in_the_harness.tools: Per-agent capability grant. Leads/orchestrator get `delegate` + `tilldone` (route and coordinate); workers get write/edit/bash (do the work); read-only validators get neither write nor delegate. Plus the `domain` field path-scopes where each tool may act (read/upsert/delete per path).
core_four_in_the_harness.why_owning_the_harness_matters: Stock tools give you one blended agent with fixed defaults. Owning the harness lets you set context, model, prompt, and tools independently for every agent, wire them into teams, run teams in parallel, and swap models on failure — the difference between prompting one agent and operating a specialized system.

infinite_ui_system.what_it_is: A multi-team agent system that generates infinite brand-consistent UI. Define a brand identity once (brand.yaml), then generate unlimited Vue variants — landing pages, dashboards, components — all visually cohesive and browseable in one Vue app. README tagline: 'Stop solving one off tasks with agents. Build systems (agent teams) that solve entire problem classes.'
infinite_ui_system.hierarchy: Brand → Product → Tree → Branch → Leaf. Brand = identity container (brand.yaml). Product = a Vue app within a brand (may override brand.yaml). Tree = a purpose category (landing, dashboard, agent-stream). Branch = a variant within a tree (status: draft|generating|validating|validated|failed). Leaf = the actual generated Vue SFC at index.vue, using only CSS custom properties from the brand config.
infinite_ui_system.zero_hardcoded_values: Every leaf uses CSS custom properties derived from brand.yaml — no hardcoded colors, fonts, spacing, or motion. Edit a token in the sidebar brand editor and all components update live; change brand.yaml and the whole product rebrands in real time.
infinite_ui_system.leaf_preview_mechanism: On the canvas, a validated branch renders as a live preview node: PreviewBranchNode.vue embeds a real <iframe> (rendered at 1280x720, CSS transform: scale() to S/M/L presets, pointer-events: none) pointing at that leaf's gallery route; that route (BranchPreview.vue) uses import.meta.glob + a dynamic <component :is> to lazy-load the exact brands/.../index.vue off disk. (Dan on camera guesses 'teleport which probably uses iframe underneath' — it is an iframe, but via import.meta.glob dynamic import; Vue's Teleport is used only in Sidebar.vue, unrelated to previews.)
infinite_ui_system.the_generate_command: /generate <brand> <product> <tree> <count> <brief> — the workhorse. Orchestrator runs an 8-step pipeline: (1) Setup scaffolds branch dirs, writes trees.yaml (status: generating) + an activity.yaml sidecar, runs Zod validation; (2) Brand loads brand.yaml context; (3) UI Generation Lead writes COUNT differentiated briefs; (4) branches assigned round-robin across UI Generation / B / C and generated in parallel; (5) Setup flips generating → validating; (6) branches validated round-robin across Validation / B / C (soft + hard); (7) failures routed back to the generating team; (8) Setup flips validating → validated/failed and clears activity.yaml.
infinite_ui_system.app_stack: Vue 3.5 (Composition API, <script setup lang=ts>), Vite 8, Pinia 3, vue-router 5, TypeScript 5.9, Bun; @vue-flow/core + @dagrejs/dagre for the canvas node graph; zod 4 + yaml for validated brand/trees manifests; vite.config.ts adds a filesystem-backed REST middleware over src/brands/ (brand/trees/activity endpoints).

multi_team_architecture.committed_shape: 1 orchestrator + 8 teams, backed by 12 unique agent prompt files, instantiated as 24 named agent slots. Teams: Setup (Setup Lead + Scaffold Worker + Structure Validator), Brand (Brand Lead + Brand Analyst), UI Generation / B / C (UI Generation Lead + Vue Generator + Animation Specialist, each), Validation / B / C (Validation Lead + Soft Validator + Hard Validator, each). The B/C teams reuse the same agent files with different colors — parallelism is pure config duplication + round-robin.

tiers.orchestrator: 1 — classifies the user request, delegates to a team lead, synthesizes the answer. Tools include delegate + tilldone. Only agent with high-autonomy skill and the {{TEAMS_BLOCK}}.
tiers.leads: 4 unique (Setup, Brand, UI Generation, Validation) — think, plan, delegate to members, synthesize; delegate + tilldone tools; zero-micro-management skill ('You are a leader — delegate, never execute.'). Their domain generally blocks writing product files (except setup-lead, widest lead write-scope).
tiers.workers_doers: 4 that write files (Scaffold Worker, Vue Generator, Animation Specialist, Brand Analyst) — write/edit/bash, precise-worker skill ('Execute exactly what your lead assigned — no improvising.'), no delegate tool. Only Scaffold Worker has delete:true.
tiers.validators_readonly: 3 (Soft Validator, Hard Validator, Structure Validator) — read/bash only, no write/edit, no delegate; report PASS/FAIL, never fix. Soft/Hard use playwright-cli (the `bowser` skill) to screenshot and test at breakpoints; Structure runs Zod on trees.yaml/brand.yaml.

multi_team_architecture.delegation_and_rules: Rule from CLAUDE.md, enforced structurally by the `tools` + `domain` front matter: 'Leads and Orchestrators are thinkers, planners and managers. They are not doers. Other than updating their own mental models, they should not write files. Workers are doers.' The phrase 'one agent, one prompt, one purpose' is Dan's verbal framing; the precise-worker skill encodes it.
multi_team_architecture.round_robin_parallelism: Orchestrator assigns branch 1 → UI Generation, branch 2 → UI Generation B, branch 3 → UI Generation C, branch 4 → UI Generation, ... and mirrors the same assignment to Validation teams. All teams write to the same filesystem; each branch directory is independent, so parallel writes do not conflict as long as each team touches only its assigned branch slugs.
multi_team_architecture.parallel_mental_model_updates: The 6 agents that live in the tripled A/B/C teams (ui-generation-lead, vue-generator, animation-specialist, validation-lead, soft-validator, hard-validator) carry the parallel-mental-model-updates skill: sibling instances share one expertise YAML, so write conflicts are 'coordination signals, not bugs' — re-read, re-apply, re-write.

step_by_step_demo: (2:16) The running system: three tiers on screen — orchestrator, leads, workers. A few agents have been modified to run Minimax 2.7 and Step 3.5 Flash next to Claude Sonnet 4.6 in their respective teams (an A/B of models).

(3:17–4:09) Tour Aegis — the 'agent security command center' brand. Each node is a full UI; the branded, largely-functional threat-detection app is one of many UIs the system built. Dan flags agents + security as a major opportunity.

(4:56–5:37) Two big ideas: (1) the agent harness matters — push/specialize outside the core four by customizing your harness; (2) scale — one agent is not enough; you want teams that remember and execute like you (observe, act, learn, iterate).

(5:40–6:08) Paste a stored, reusable prompt into the orchestrator chat to create a net-new application. Single orchestrator interface; input does not scale with agent count. The orchestrator @-mentions the Setup team with a full prompt — it has been taught to prompt-engineer.
(6:31–6:47) The till-done list enhancement: agents work until all tasks are complete. Layout: scale on the left, structure/communication on the right, chat on top.

(6:49–7:12) Orchestrator and leads delegate, they don't work. Setup lead reads key files, understands the job, and delegates to the Scaffold Worker; scaffolding begins on the new Sonnet/Opus 1M-context models.
(8:57–9:48) Setup completes → deploy horizontally-scaled UI Generation teams A, B, C in parallel. Leads pick up and delegate the building to workers. Three-tier architecture for maximum value.
(9:49–10:11) A reduced team is running (some agents dropped for filming; e.g. a brand analyst). X marks appear when an agent steps out of its domain.
(10:30–11:03) Tour the workspace: three brands (Aegis, Agentix, Indydevdan) → products → trees with branches → leaves. 'This team operates this product.'

(12:10–13:20) Check the teams: team C (Sonnet) is working; teams A and B (open-source models) return 'no response.' Reason to run multiple teams/models; a model-rotation system could swap a failing model out.

(13:22–13:50) The leads break the rule: 'I need to produce the output to fulfill the task myself.' Their workers (open-source) are non-functional, so the leads write the components themselves — very team-lead-like emergent behavior.

(14:37–16:00) Tour the harness/codebase: your own file structure (.pi/multi-team). The agents file lists every agent; the expertise files hold each agent's ~7K-token, self-maintained mental model ('I don't touch this file ever').
(16:00–17:44) The multi-team config shows shared context, the orchestrator path, and the full team. Search 'name': ~15 agents in the full team, ~9 in the min version running now.

(17:45–18:58) Open the Vue Generator system prompt (open-source version, model: stepfun/step-3.5-flash). Front matter is where the magic happens: expertise file, hot-loaded skills, tools, and domain (focused operating area). One agent, one prompt, one purpose.

(18:59–19:52) Leads take over validation too as workers keep failing; the till-done system lets orchestrator and leads coordinate — 'two variants need fixes, let me delegate back to the correct teams.'

(19:59–20:31) Full control over the core four (context, model, prompt, tools) — which requires control of the harness. Come into the multi-team file and build any specialized team you want; scale it across domains.

(20:42–22:31) Reusable prompts composed against teams. The /generate command: parameters brand, product, tree, count, prompt; consistent Variables / Instructions / Workflow format; 'delegate' is a tool; 80–90% of work is a workflow the orchestrator runs top to bottom.
(22:38–23:05) Pipeline done: three versions generated; four (open-source) agents bombed. Value of multiple models/teams so a failing agent's work is picked up.

(23:07–25:00) Browse the three new Aegis agent-stream UIs — glassmorphism panel, timeline stack, compact dashboard — via iframe previews. Real, brand-consistent, functional: live agent chat where the Sentinel agent flags an unusual login pattern; filtering and animations.
(25:00–26:15) At scale, one prompt is not enough. Big themes to focus on: harness engineering, multi-agent orchestration, and trust + scale.

(26:25–31:00) Agentic Horizon pitch: the trilogy (CEO agents → lead agents → UI agents), member assets, 'you are the bottleneck,' template your engineering into system prompts / skills / reusable prompts.
(31:00–32:26) Solve problem classes not tasks. Claude Code as meta agent (~80%) building systems that build systems. The theme of 2026 is trust at scale.

prerequisites_tools: The Pi coding agent (pi.dev) — the granular-control agent harness Dan specializes
The Multi-Team Agentic Coding system + the `teams` shell alias (member asset; ui-agents runs on top of it)
Claude Code (the meta-builder / bootloader that runs .claude/commands, e.g. /install)
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (and, for the open-source A/B, OpenRouter / provider keys for Minimax and Step)
An IDE (Dan uses VS Code), a terminal

what_student_must_internalize: The durable edge is the harness, not the model. Models commoditize; deterministic code + caching + orchestration + prompts + skills + model control are what a $2.5B business is built on.
Stop solving one-off tasks. Build a team of agents that operates a whole problem class on your behalf — because 80–90% of work is a repeatable workflow.
Three tiers: orchestrator and leads think, plan, and delegate (they don't write files); workers do. Enforce it structurally with per-agent tools + domain, not just prose.
Your input must not scale with agent count. One orchestrator interface; horizontal team scaling behind it.

Owning the harness means owning the core four per agent: context (shared + expertise), model (per-agent, swappable), prompt (system + reusable workflow), tools (delegate/tilldone vs write/edit vs read-only) — plus domain path-scoping.
Front matter is the specialization surface: expertise (mental model), skills (hot-loaded behavior), tools, domain. One agent, one prompt, one purpose.
Agents that keep persistent mental models compound across sessions — but they start empty and grow at runtime; the human doesn't hand-write them.

Reliability is a first-class concern: heterogeneous models let you A/B and rotate, and multi-team redundancy means a failed model's work gets picked up (in the demo, leads finish when open-source workers die).
Claude Code stays in the loop as the meta-agent that builds the system that builds the system — in ands, not ors.
The goal is trust at scale: increase, over time, how much work you trust your agents to do — until they operate your product end to end.
common_weak_student_failures: Hearing 'own the harness' as 'abandon Claude Code.' Dan spends ~80% of his time in Claude Code as the meta-builder; the harness runs the product. It's 'in ands not ors.'
Believing the mental models ship full of learned knowledge. In the committed repo every expertise/*.yaml is a one-line stub; the 7K-token model on screen is runtime state.

Assuming all 12 agents run open-source models because the video A/Bs them. On disk every agent is anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6; the open-source swaps (stepfun/step-3.5-flash, openrouter/minimax/minimax-m2.7) were live edits not committed.
Reading the demo's failures as the idea failing. The failures prove the thesis: owning the harness makes a broken model survivable — leads finish the task and models can be rotated.

Thinking leads/orchestrator are idle because 'they don't work.' Their job is classify → delegate → synthesize; the write-block is enforced by domain permissions, and they still coordinate the whole run.
Treating /generate as a single prompt. It is an 8-step, multi-team, round-robin, validated pipeline — the value is the workflow, not the sentence.
Trusting Dan's on-camera 'teleport' guess for leaf previews. The real mechanism is an iframe + import.meta.glob dynamic <component :is>; Teleport is only used in the Sidebar.
Chasing the Aegis UI as the point. Aegis is the demo domain; the transferable lesson is the owned multi-team harness that generated it.
Adding agents and expecting the system to get easier to drive without keeping the single-orchestrator interface — re-introducing yourself as the bottleneck.
Fixating on the exact model IDs and counts (Sonnet 4.6, Minimax 2.7, '15/9 agents'). These are period/live-demo specifics; the durable ideas are harness + orchestration + trust.
teach_back_prompt: Explain to a colleague, without notes: (1) what the Claude Code leak's real signal is and why 'the harness is the product' means models are commoditizing while harness engineering is the skill to invest in; (2) the three-tier orchestrator → leads → workers architecture, why leads/orchestrator don't write files, and how the repo enforces that with `tools` + `domain` front matter; (3) how a single agent's front matter (expertise + skills + tools + domain) gives you control of the core four per agent, and what 'one agent, one prompt, one purpose' buys you; and (4) why the demo's open-source model failures — and the leads writing components themselves — are evidence FOR the tactic, not against it. Finish by resolving the paradox: how does owning a harness and running teams of agents let you do LESS prompting while doing MORE work?

retrieval_questions.q: What did the Claude Code source-code leak actually signal, according to Dan?
retrieval_questions.a: That the agent harness — not the model — is the product. A $2.5B ARR business is built on the harness (deterministic code, token caching, agent orchestration, prompts, skills, model control), while the model on top is being commoditized.

retrieval_questions.q: Name the six components of the agent harness Dan lists.
retrieval_questions.a: Deterministic code, token caching, agent orchestration, prompts, skills, and model control.

retrieval_questions.q: What is the difference between vibe coding, single-agent agentic coding, and harness engineering?
retrieval_questions.a: Vibe coding = prompt a model to make code. Single-agent agentic coding = one agent (e.g. Claude Code) running tool chains. Harness engineering = you own the harness and run specialized teams of agents that solve whole problem classes.

retrieval_questions.q: Why must your input to the system not scale with the number of agents?
retrieval_questions.a: Because if driving the system got harder with every agent added, the human becomes the bottleneck. Teams scale horizontally, but you always talk to one orchestrator.

retrieval_questions.q: In the three-tier architecture, who writes files and who doesn't — and how is it enforced?
retrieval_questions.a: Workers write files; orchestrator and leads don't (they think, plan, delegate). It's enforced structurally by front matter: leads/orchestrator get delegate + tilldone but their `domain` blocks writing product files; workers get write/edit/bash.

retrieval_questions.q: What four things live in an agent's front matter, and what does each control?
retrieval_questions.a: expertise (the agent's persistent mental model), skills (hot-loaded behavior), tools (its capabilities, e.g. delegate/tilldone vs write/edit), and domain (the exact paths it may read/upsert/delete). Together they control the core four per agent.

retrieval_questions.q: How do the agents 'learn,' and what's the catch about the committed repo?
retrieval_questions.a: Each agent maintains its own YAML expertise file (mental model), read at task start and updated after work via a ~75-line skill; it compounds across sessions (capped at max-lines: 10000). Catch: in the committed repo all 12 files are empty one-line stubs — the ~7K-token model shown on screen is runtime state.

retrieval_questions.q: What is a 'till-done' list, and where does it actually come from?
retrieval_questions.a: Not a to-do or to-done list — a list the agents work until every task is complete. It's an orchestrator capability (the `tilldone` tool in orchestrator.md), used autonomously; the committed generate.md deliberately omits a task list to stress-test coordination.

retrieval_questions.q: The demo's open-source teams (Minimax, Step) failed. Why is that evidence FOR the tactic?
retrieval_questions.a: Because owning the harness made it survivable: the leads (Claude) picked up the dead workers' tasks and finished them, and Dan notes a model-rotation system could swap failing models out. Redundancy across models/teams keeps the pipeline delivering.

retrieval_questions.q: What does the /generate command take, and roughly what does it do?
retrieval_questions.a: /generate <brand> <product> <tree> <count> <brief>. The orchestrator runs an 8-step pipeline: Setup scaffolds → Brand loads context → UI Gen writes N briefs → round-robin generate across teams A/B/C → Setup marks validating → round-robin validate across A/B/C → fix failures → Setup finalizes statuses.

retrieval_questions.q: What is the Brand → Product → Tree → Branch → Leaf hierarchy?
retrieval_questions.a: Brand = identity container (brand.yaml). Product = a Vue app in a brand. Tree = a purpose category (e.g. landing, agent-stream). Branch = a variant (status draft→validated). Leaf = the generated index.vue SFC using only brand CSS custom properties.

retrieval_questions.q: How is a leaf UI actually previewed on the canvas (vs Dan's guess)?
retrieval_questions.a: A validated branch renders as an <iframe> (1280x720, CSS-scaled, pointer-events:none) pointing at the leaf's gallery route, which uses import.meta.glob + dynamic <component :is> to load the SFC. Dan guesses 'teleport'; it's iframe + glob (Teleport is only in the Sidebar).

retrieval_questions.q: Why does Dan still spend ~80% of his time in Claude Code?
retrieval_questions.a: As a meta-agent / meta-builder — building the systems (teams of agents, AI developer workflows) that then operate the product. Claude Code builds the system that builds the system; the specialized Pi harness runs it.

retrieval_questions.q: What are the two big skills and the underlying theme Dan names?
retrieval_questions.a: Skills: harness engineering and multi-agent orchestration. Underlying theme: trust and scale — the theme of 2026 is increasing the trust you place in your agents to do larger scales of work over time.

current_practice_gaps.gap: What you get (committed asset) vs what you saw (live demo)
current_practice_gaps.why: The lesson is a live showcase from a working copy that includes an agents-os/ tree of open-source agent variants, a multi-team-config-min.yaml, populated 7K-token mental models, and extra brands. The committed member asset ships a single Claude-Sonnet config, empty mental-model stubs, and one brand (aegis). A reader who clones it should expect to run all-Claude teams and grow the mental models themselves. The concept maps 1:1; the on-screen artifacts are a superset.

current_practice_gaps.gap: Model landscape is period-specific and moves fast
current_practice_gaps.why: Claude Sonnet 4.6 / Opus 4.6, Minimax M2.7, Step 3.5 Flash, and the 1M-context Sonnet/Opus are April-2026 specifics; the 'Mythos model' is a leak-era reference. The durable point — the harness lets you set and rotate models per agent — outlives every one of these IDs. Re-verify model names at publish.

current_practice_gaps.gap: The mainstream tool is absorbing harness features
current_practice_gaps.why: The 'own the harness with Pi' thesis is sharpest when the mainstream tool is a black box. But Claude Code itself now exposes subagents, hooks, skills, plugins, output styles, and settings layering — much of the harness surface Dan builds in Pi. The lesson's deeper claim survives: whoever controls context/model/prompt/tools + orchestration wins; the question is how much you build yourself vs configure in a tool that's catching up.

current_practice_gaps.gap: Till-done in the demo vs the committed prompt
current_practice_gaps.why: On screen the orchestrator runs a TillDone list ([1/8] → [11/11]) via its tilldone tool. The committed generate.md deliberately carries NO task list (per specs/parallel-team-duplication.md) to test whether the orchestrator can coordinate 3 parallel teams from context + trees.yaml + activity.yaml alone. Both are true; the till-done is an orchestrator capability, not part of the /generate prompt.

current_practice_gaps.gap: Leaf-preview mechanism vs Dan's on-camera guess
current_practice_gaps.why: Dan says the previews use 'teleport which probably uses iframe underneath.' The actual mechanism is a real <iframe> (1280x720, CSS-scaled) into the leaf's gallery route, which uses import.meta.glob + a dynamic <component :is>. Vue's Teleport appears only in Sidebar.vue. A reader auditing the code should not go looking for Teleport in the preview path.
